name: Tom Cotton
what: Arkansas Advocate reported that Cotton, like his two challengers, said in an interview that he supports giving Arkansans a vote on whether a data center is built near them, and that AI companies should be transparent about data centers' impacts on communities. This is the reporter's paraphrase of a September interview with 40/29 News; Cotton did not answer the Advocate's own questions.
source_name: Arkansas Advocate (via News From The States)

name: Ashley Moody
what: Said on Fox News' 'Sunday Morning Futures' that it should be up to the people of a community or a state to decide whether to host data centers, and that companies need to make their case, including that residents will not bear costs or environmental and health effects. Florida Politics summarised this as cities and counties deciding.

name: Jon Ossoff
what: Launched an investigation into data centers' impact on Georgians' power bills.
source_name: Sen. Ossoff investigates Georgia data centers' impact on power bills (2026)

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Led letters to ISO New England and to NARUC on shielding ratepayers from data-center costs; released a draft bill requiring a federal public-interest certificate before a data center is permitted.
source_name: Sen. Markey — discussion draft, Protecting Communities from Data Center Impacts Act (2026)

name: Cory A. Booker
what: Cosponsored the Power for the People Act, making data-center operators pay the grid costs they create.
source_name: Sen. Welch joins bill so Americans aren't footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Jeff Merkley
what: With Wyden, wrote Oregon's data center advisory committee listing constituent concerns on energy demand, consumer costs, water, noise and farmland.
source_name: Sens. Wyden & Merkley ask Oregon data center advisory committee to weigh Oregonians' concerns (2026)

name: Jack Reed
what: Signed the New England senators' letter asking ISO New England how it will shield residential ratepayers from data-center-driven price increases.
source_name: Sens. Reed & Whitehouse seek answers on how regional data centers could drive up costs (2026)

name: Mark R. Warner
what: Cosponsored legislation so Virginians aren't stuck footing data-center utility costs, and introduced an energy/water disclosure bill.
source_name: Sen. Warner — bill so Virginians aren't stuck footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Mary Peltola
what: Newsweek reported (reporter's paraphrase, linked to a Facebook video, not a direct quote) that Peltola during the campaign emphasized that local communities should have a voice in the data-center discussion and that data centers should pay their own way. Newsweek said it had contacted her campaign; no response is reported.

name: Adam Hamilton
what: Campaign issues page lists 'Require data centers to pay their fair share of electricity costs' under his affordability agenda, saying the companies behind data centers should cover their costs instead of burdening ratepayers and should earn the support of the towns and counties they move into, and that he would propose binding rules and legislation where others support voluntary pledges.

name: Andy Barr
what: Campaign energy plan (PDF) lists 'Support AI data centers and advanced manufacturing that depend on affordable, nonstop power' among its legislative aims, alongside speeding permits for power plants and transmission lines, and says the plan will lower energy costs for Kentuckians.
source_name: Andy Barr for Senate, 'Plan to Revive Coal Jobs and Power the Technologies of the Future'

name: Julia Letlow
what: Spoke at the public launch event for Meta's Richland Parish data center, which Gulf States Newsroom says came six months after she signed the NDA, and championed the project. The page gives no date for the event.
source_name: Gulf States Newsroom via Louisiana Illuminator

name: Troy Jackson
what: Campaign statement to Newsweek set conditions for data centers coming to Maine: create good-paying union jobs, pay their fair share, protect natural resources and work with local communities; the campaign said Maine families should not subsidize the energy needs of some of the richest corporations in the world.

name: Troy Jackson
what: Newsweek reported that earlier in 2026, while campaigning for governor, he criticised Gov. Mills's veto of the data-center moratorium and said a pause was needed.

name: Troy Jackson
what: The American Prospect reported that at a forum the week of Oct. 12 Jackson and Collins agreed data centers must not affect water usage or force ratepayers to pay more for electricity and that local agreements were key (reporter's paraphrase, not a direct quote).

name: Troy Jackson
what: Roll Call reported that in a debate with Collins the week before Oct. 19 he called for "real guardrails" on data centers and backed safeguards so they would not raise power bills for other customers or harm local water supplies.

name: Abdul El-Sayed
what: At a press conference at a data-center site in Saline (July 2026; the campaign release gives no calendar date), said that until terms of engagement exist at the federal level he would back local and state officials in not approving more data centers, and that "a moratorium makes sense" for states or localities.

name: Abdul El-Sayed
what: Newsweek reported, citing a CBS 60 Minutes appearance, that he said "we need local and state moratoriums" until federal rules exist, that data centers "cannot touch our waterways at all", should use "all union labor", and need community benefits agreements negotiated transparently with local communities. The page gives no date for the remarks (published around the start of November 2026).

name: Abdul El-Sayed
what: Roll Call reported that at the Michigan Senate general-election debate in October he said he supports "terms of engagement" for data centers, without saying in the debate what those terms should be.

name: James Talarico
what: At a CNN town hall, per Newsweek, said he had rolled out a plan to 'crack down on these giant data center companies': 'force them to pay for their own energy instead of jacking up our utility bills,' 'force them to recycle their water,' and 'force them to get the consent of the people who live in these communities before they start building.'

name: Jeff Merkley
what: In a statement on Senate passage of the permitting bill, said he could not support it and listed among his concerns that it deregulated the buildout of data centers and allowed data centers to be built on public lands; said Senate Republicans blocked votes on amendments addressing these issues; and said that as incoming EPW chairman he wants permitting legislation to go through committee in 2027.

name: Tom Cotton
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33) - a permitting bill whose supporters say it requires data centers to pay for the grid costs they create. No statement from Cotton about this vote was found.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 270 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Voted to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (H.R. 2347 as amended; Senate vote 270, passed 62-33). His release says that, according to independent analysis, the bill would require data centers to pay for the increased grid and energy costs they create.

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Wrote to Sen. Schumer and Sen. Van Hollen, candidates for Senate Democratic leader, pressing for an agenda on AI safety, affordability and accountability; the letter cites families' rising energy bills and farmers' concern about data centers draining limited water. The letter's asks are about AI regulation generally, not a specific data-center measure.

name: Christopher A. Coons
what: Voted for Senate passage of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (H.R. 2347 as amended; Senate vote 270, 62-33) and said it would ensure data centers pay more than their fair share in the communities they impact. He said he had fought unsuccessfully for amendments to the bill's environmental and historic-preservation provisions.

name: Ashley Moody
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33) - a permitting bill whose supporters say it requires data centers to pay for the grid costs they create. No statement from Moody about this vote was found.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 270 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: Jon Ossoff
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33) - a permitting bill whose supporters say it requires data centers to pay for the grid costs they create and whose critics say it weakens environmental and historic-preservation review. He had voted Yea on the earlier procedural votes and on the substitute amendment. No statement from Ossoff explaining the vote was found.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 270 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: James E. Risch
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33), the vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting bill whose sponsors say it makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they cause.

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Statement after the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, calling it an energy permitting bill that will let mines, pipelines, power plants and data centers be approved without concern for public health or public consent, and a win for Big Tech and Big Oil.

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33), the vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting bill whose sponsors say it makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they cause.

name: Pete Ricketts
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (Senate vote 270, passed 62-33), the vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, a permitting bill whose sponsors say it makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they cause.

name: Cory A. Booker
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the vehicle for the Senate's bipartisan permitting bill (referred to on the floor as BAAJA), which passed 62-33. In the floor debate recorded on the same pages, supporter Sen. Whitehouse said the bill would force data centers to pay for the costs they impose on the grid, while opponent Sen. Merkley said it puts the pedal to the floor on data centers. The pages record no statement by Booker.

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the vehicle for the permitting bill, which passed 62-33.

name: Jeff Merkley
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (the vehicle for the permitting bill), which passed 62-33.

name: Jeff Merkley
what: On the Senate floor, objected to the unanimous-consent agreement on amendment votes for the permitting bill. He said the bill 'puts the pedal to the floor on data centers', described his amendment to stop jet-engine generators powering data centers from being exempted from clean air and noise provisions, and backed Sen. Wyden's amendment to keep data centers off public lands; his request to add those amendments was objected to.

name: Jack Reed
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended, the vehicle for the Senate's bipartisan permitting bill, which passed 62-33. In the floor debate on the same pages, co-author Sen. Whitehouse said the bill would force data centers to pay for the costs they impose on the grid, while Sen. Merkley said it puts the pedal to the floor on data centers. The pages record no statement by Reed.

name: Mike Rounds
what: Voted Nay on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (the legislative vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act), which passed 62-33. He also voted Nay on the Capito substitute amendment (vote 267, 2026-11-18) and on the cloture votes (257, 264, 268).

name: Bill Hagerty
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (the legislative vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act), which passed 62-33; also Yea on the Capito substitute amendment (vote 267) and the related cloture votes (257, 264, 268).

name: Mark R. Warner
what: Voted Yea on Senate passage of H.R. 2347 as amended (the legislative vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the permitting bill whose sponsors say it makes data centers pay for the grid upgrades they cause), which passed 62-33; also Yea on the Capito substitute (vote 267) and the related cloture votes (257, 264, 268).

name: Shelley Moore Capito
what: The Senate passed her bill 62-33 (Capito Yea; the substitute adopted the day before was Capito Amdt. No. 6883). WOWK reported that sponsors said the bill does not touch data-center permitting but does require data centers to pay for the increased cost of their energy consumption.

name: Mike Rounds
what: Was the lone Republican to vote against advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. His statement objected that the bill would transfer contested transmission-line siting cases to FERC if not resolved within 12 months, 'giving a weighted advantage to the developer.' The article does not mention data centers.

name: Shelley Moore Capito
what: In Senate floor remarks as the Senate advanced BAAJA 73-25, said the bill's energy section includes the Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation that will make potential data centers pay their own way instead of consumers facing higher utility bills. The release says she introduced BAAJA with Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich.

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (a permitting bill) and said the deal would make data centers pay their fair share, while saying the bill should be strengthened with Tribal Nations and environmental groups. Senate vote 257 (cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, 73-25) records him as Yea.

name: Christopher A. Coons
what: Announced he would support the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, a permitting bill, saying it ensures data centers pay their fair share and pay for upgrades to electricity systems; said he expected an amendment process to improve it. Senate vote 257 the same day (cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, 73-25) records him as Yea.

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: Voted against advancing the Senate permitting bill (the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act) in the Nov. 9 procedural vote, saying he shares concerns raised by tribal leaders and environmentalists and could not support advancing the bill in its current form. Source NM reports that sponsor Sen. Heinrich says the bill would hold data centers financially liable for new costs they impose on energy grids; Luján's statement as quoted does not mention data centers.

name: Jeff Merkley
what: In a statement before the first procedural vote on the permitting bill, said data centers should pay their fair share for the resources they use and praised those portions of the bill, but said he would vote against it because it could make it easier to build data centers powered by behind-the-meter natural gas plants and eliminates tools states and localities use to fight new data centers.

name: Shelley Moore Capito
what: With Sens. Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich, released the substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026. In the release Heinrich (not Capito) says the bill 'makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause'; Capito's own quote urges swift passage 'to make life more affordable for American families.'

name: Mark R. Warner
what: In a post-election interview with WJLA, called for a federal baseline under which a data center of any size must bring its own power and its own water.

name: Annie Andrews
what: In WSOC-TV's post-election report, quoted saying 'If a community says no, the answer is no,' and that she has called for a two-year moratorium on data-center development to empower local communities and local elected officials to negotiate with the companies.

name: Chris Pappas
what: NHPR's election guide reports that both Pappas and his Republican opponent John E. Sununu have said they support a state-level moratorium on data center construction. This is NHPR's characterisation; the page carries no direct Pappas quote on a moratorium.

name: Jeff Merkley
what: With Sens. Wyden and Padilla, wrote to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum demanding answers about his role in helping broker deals to build data centers on public lands, after the department released calendars showing meetings with data center developers.

name: Annie Andrews
what: Publicly criticised outside spending for her opponent by what she described as data-center-linked super PACs, saying Graham 'has repeatedly said we have to have data centers and we need to build data centers here.' The dollar figures in the story are Andrews' own claims as reported by WACH, not independently verified there.

name: Sherrod Brown
what: At a Cleveland rally, dismissed Husted's Ratepayer Protection Act as 'toothless', called Husted 'the face of data centers', and said Husted gave data-center corporations $2.5 billion in tax dollars while utility bills rose. The figures are Brown's claims as quoted.

name: Sherrod Brown
what: Told News 5 Cleveland, two weeks before the election, that his position is to take away data-center tax subsidies, let local communities give input and keep data centers out where they are not wanted, and never have electric ratepayers pay for data centers' electricity. In the same story, answering Husted's charge of hypocrisy, he said he had supported one data center around 2015-2016, when there were no big tax subsidies and the local communities knew about it.

name: Andy Barr
what: In the only televised Senate debate (WKYT), said Kentuckians should not pay higher utility bills if a data center moves into their town (reporter's paraphrase), that the U.S. must win the AI race against China, and that he believes in local control.
source_name: Yahoo News (syndicated; byline McKenna Horsley, original outlet not shown on the page)

name: Kurt Alme
what: NBC Montana's roundup of candidate positions quoted him saying data-center companies need to pay their own way and hire local jobs, cannot have adverse impacts on water, and that the decision should be left to local communities. The article says he supports the "Ratepayer Protection Act" (reporter's paraphrase).

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: Joined Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden and five other senators in a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking Meta to justify its use of federal research and development tax credits to fund its buildout of AI data centers.

name: Pete Ricketts
what: In a release on his AI record, listed the Ratepayer Protection Act among legislation he has championed, describing it as giving states and local communities leverage to negotiate on data centers.

name: Andy Barr
what: Told Spectrum News 1, in a campaign profile, that the country needs more data centers and more affordable, reliable power, and that localities should decide whether to host them. The article also says that in February he supported the administration's loosening of emission standards for coal-fired power plants while advocating for more hyper-scale data centers (reporter's characterisation).

name: Chris Pappas
what: Signed a bipartisan House letter, led by Reps. Panetta and Steube, to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent expressing concern about reports that Meta is seeking to use the federal research tax credit for its data center buildout. Panetta's release lists Chris Pappas (NH-01) among the signers.

name: Juliana Stratton
what: Asked on Illinois Public Media's The 21st Show about a federal role in regulating data-center growth, said data centers 'have to pay their fair share', must invest in the electric grid, that Illinoisans cannot be made to shoulder the burden of the expansion, and that the state put a pause on tax incentives to slow things down. She said that at the federal level 'we need to again look at what the implications are' and named no federal bill.

name: Juliana Stratton
what: In the same interview, said developers must be transparent with communities and that communities must have the chance to voice concerns, with 'community voice being right at the center', and that water and other natural resources should be protected through regulation.

name: Josh Turek
what: At the second and final debate (WHO-TV), Radio Iowa reported that both Hinson and Turek said local officials should decide where data centers may be built, and that both oppose a federal moratorium on data center construction. Reporter's paraphrase.

name: Josh Turek
what: WOI's report on the second debate says Hinson was more open to data center development agreements than Turek, and that both opposed a statewide moratorium on data centers. Reporter's characterisation; no Turek quote.

name: Troy Jackson
what: At an Oct. 13 debate with Sen. Collins, said: "I'm not really supportive of data centers, but I understand they're maybe something that we have to deal with," and that he is "very much in favor of making sure the federal government or the state of Maine puts guardrails on these things." Newsweek reported he said data centers in Maine must not raise electricity rates or harm water quality and should be slowed down so people can understand them.

name: Kurt Alme
what: At the Montana Broadcasters Association U.S. Senate debate in Bozeman, said he would work for transparency, clear guardrails and for Montana communities to be heard. The Daily Montanan reported he said AI companies building data centers should be transparent about their costs to the community, pay their own way, hire locally, and not harm water supplies, water quality or electricity rates (paraphrase).

name: Annie Andrews
what: At the Oct. 11 SC ETV debate, proposed a two-year moratorium; per the Gazette's paraphrase, regulations developed during the pause should ensure data centers pay for themselves so customers' rates do not go up. She said she wants a 'return to real local control' and accused her opponent of wanting to build data centers 'faster and faster.'

name: Annie Andrews
what: In the same debate, as quoted by WRDW, said data centers are being built in communities' backyards without community input.

name: Chris Pappas
what: In an NHPR candidate interview, said communities should be given power over data center development, that a town facing a proposal should have every opportunity to vet and reject it, and that ratepayers should not be on the hook for massive data center development in New Hampshire or anywhere else.

name: Jon Ossoff
what: In the first Senate debate with Rep. Mike Collins (Atlanta News First / Gray Media, Thursday Oct. 8, 2026), asked how he would keep data-center strain on the grid from raising utility bills, said no Georgia family or small business should pay more to subsidize data centers' energy consumption and that no local community should have data centers imposed on it. He then said the 2025 budget bill gave $70 billion to data center developers (his figure) and challenged Collins to commit to repealing what he called 'that data center tax scam'.

name: Josh Turek
what: At the Iowa PBS debate, KCCI reported that both candidates said data centers should not drive up utility costs, and that Turek called for more federal regulation, including requiring data centers to use closed-loop cooling systems to reduce water use. This is the reporter's paraphrase, not a direct quote.

name: Josh Turek
what: Gray Media's report on the same Iowa PBS debate says the two candidates agreed that data centers should not get tax breaks. The article attributes this to both candidates jointly and gives no direct quote from Turek.
source_name: KTTC (Gray Media Iowa State Capitol Bureau)

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: At a Denver discussion with residents and energy-assistance leaders, where residents raised concerns about footing the bill for data centers, his office said he spoke about the need to shield ratepayers from paying for Big Tech's data center infrastructure (office summary, no direct quote).

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Signed, with Sens. Kelly and Whitehouse, a letter opposing the EPA's proposal to eliminate the 30-day mandatory public notice period for proposed facilities, such as data centers, that may affect air quality.

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: In a KVIA voter-guide questionnaire, said data centers should not use drinking water or agricultural water, should be required to generate their own power rather than strain the grid, and that New Mexicans should not pay a penny more for electricity.

name: Julia Letlow
what: Louisiana Illuminator's roundup of data centers in the state's congressional races reports that Letlow cited her House vote for the Ratepayer Protection Act as proof of her support for holding data centers responsible for their promises. This is the reporter's paraphrase; the article carries no direct Letlow quote and does not say where or when she said it. (The page misspells her name 'Lettow'.)

name: Pete Ricketts
what: In his weekly column, wrote that data centers "shouldn't get a free pass", that he supports the Ratepayer Protection Act, that local communities should set the terms before a data center is built and should have a choice in allowing them, and that communities could negotiate for things like lower property taxes. He also wrote that the U.S. needs to beat China in the AI race.

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Statement on the bipartisan permitting reform proposal, saying data center developers are using ratepayers to subsidize their operations and that he was still reviewing the text.

name: Tom Cotton
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (Senate vote 254). The motion was rejected 57-43, short of the 60 required.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Voted Nay on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (Senate vote 254); the motion was rejected 57-43.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Explained his opposition to the Ratepayer Protection Act: he said it asks states to consider protections for ratepayers but does not require them, and his office said Senate Democrats had pushed a provision that would have required the largest new power users to pay their fair share to connect.

name: Christopher A. Coons
what: Voted Nay on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (Senate vote 254); the motion was rejected 57-43.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: Ashley Moody
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (Senate vote 254); the motion was rejected 57-43.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: Ashley Moody
what: After the cloture vote failed, issued a statement faulting Senate Democrats for blocking the Ratepayer Protection Act (and a separate congressional stock-trading bill).

name: Jon Ossoff
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act (Senate vote 254); the motion was rejected 57-43. Roll Call reported he was one of four Democrats to support it.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd session)

name: James E. Risch
what: Voted Yea on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act, on recovering the full incremental cost of upgrades that serve large-load customers). The motion was rejected 57-43, with 60 needed.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254, 119th Congress 2nd Session

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Voted Nay on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act). The motion was rejected 57-43, with 60 needed. No Markey statement explaining the vote was found.
source_name: U.S. Senate roll call vote 254, 119th Congress 2nd Session

name: Edward J. Markey
what: Released a report, 'The EPA's Data Center Disaster', on EPA rollbacks of air, water and chemical rules that he says make it easier to build data centers and the fossil fuel infrastructure that powers them.

name: Pete Ricketts
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (Senate Vote No. 254). The motion was rejected 57-43, short of the 60 votes needed.

name: Cory A. Booker
what: Voted Nay on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act). Cloture was rejected 57-43, with 60 votes required, so the Senate did not take up the bill.
source_name: U.S. Senate Roll Call Vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd Session)

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: With Sens. Heinrich, Kelly and Cantwell, wrote to NARUC's president and first vice president asking that every state utility commission adopt a dedicated rate rider applying to every large data center, so that data centers pay the full cost of the generation, transmission and distribution built to serve them. The letter asks NARUC to take the issue up at its November annual meeting and report back.

name: Ben Ray Luján
what: Voted Nay on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act). Cloture was rejected 57-43, with 60 votes required.
source_name: U.S. Senate Roll Call Vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd Session)

name: Jeff Merkley
what: Voted Nay on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act). Cloture was rejected 57-43, with 60 votes required.
source_name: U.S. Senate Roll Call Vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd Session)

name: Jack Reed
what: Voted Nay on the motion to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act). Cloture was rejected 57-43, with 60 votes required.
source_name: U.S. Senate Roll Call Vote 254 (119th Congress, 2nd Session)

name: Mike Rounds
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, described on the Senate vote page as a bill to establish a federal standard on recovering the full incremental costs of upgrades that serve large-load customers. The motion failed 57-43.

name: Bill Hagerty
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, described on the Senate vote page as a bill to establish a federal standard on recovering the full incremental costs of upgrades that serve large-load customers. The motion failed 57-43.

name: Mark R. Warner
what: Voted Nay on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340 (the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act, described on the Senate page as establishing a federal standard on recovering the full incremental costs of upgrades serving large-load customers). The motion failed 57-43. Newsweek reported (paraphrase, no direct quote) that he said the bill merely directs states to consider a standard and that Congress needs broader requirements on electricity costs, water, transparency and community impacts.

name: Shelley Moore Capito
what: Voted Yea on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 9340, described on the Senate vote page as a bill to establish a federal standard on recovering the full incremental costs of upgrades that serve large-load customers. The motion failed 57-43.

name: Andy Barr
what: Campaign statement to WPSD, responding to Booker's attacks over the Paducah project, saying local communities rather than Washington should decide whether data centers are built.

name: James Talarico
what: FOX 4 summarised his plan as: repeal tax incentives for data centers, more local say, an 'AI Dividend' giving every American a share of AI company profits, AI companies paying for their own electricity infrastructure, and accountability for water pollution plus paying for their own water infrastructure (all reporter paraphrase of the plan).

name: John W. Hickenlooper
what: Sent a letter to President Trump ahead of a White House meeting with technology executives; his office lists among the things he called on Trump and technology leaders to work with Congress on: protecting communities from the costs of the AI buildout, including ensuring massive data centers pay their own way for their energy consumption.

name: Cory A. Booker
what: Cosponsored Senate Amendment 6840 (Van Hollen) to H.R. 9340, the House-passed Ratepayer Protection Act. The amendment, which was ordered to lie on the table, adds a sense of Congress that ratepayers should not be forced to take on the financial risks and costs of infrastructure for data centers and that data center owners should be held accountable for the energy costs they cause.

name: Mark R. Warner
what: Submitted Senate Amendment 6837 to H.R. 9340 (the Ratepayer Protection Act), which would have added a section exempting AI data centers from bonus depreciation (unless LEED Gold/Platinum or an equivalent standard) and a section requiring disclosures from data centers with power demand of 25 megawatts or more. The amendment was ordered to lie on the table; congress.gov lists no further action.

name: Annie Andrews

name: Ashley Moody
what: Announced her cosponsorship of the Ratepayer Protection Act and criticized Senate Democrats for blocking it. name: Adam Hamilton
what: In a statement quoted in a fact-check of the Senate candidates' data-center positions, said data-center builders should not receive tax breaks.

name: Scott Colom

name: Scott Colom

name: Tom Cotton

name: Suhas Subramanyam

name: Sherrod Brown

name: Pete Ricketts

name: Sherrod Brown
what: Speaking with reporters in Westerville, listed what he wants on data centers: local input on siting, union labor to build them, no over-the-top tax breaks for big tech companies, and Ohioans not paying the electric bills of out-of-state corporations. name: John W. Hickenlooper

name: Chellie Pingree
what: Cosponsor of H.R. 9442, the AI Data Center Moratorium Act (sponsor Rep. Ocasio-Cortez), added 09/14/2026.

name: Adam Hamilton
what: At the Kansas State Fair debate with Sen. Marshall, the Hutch Post reported that Hamilton agreed guardrails are needed on AI while the U.S. keeps competing with China and Russia, and questioned how Marshall could support both data-center tax benefits and local moratoriums. Reporter's paraphrase; the only direct quote is that this may be 'one place where we both agree.'

name: Troy Downing
what: Stated 'Data centers can bring investment and opportunity to Montana, but these decisions should be made by the communities that will live with them'; called for 'light-touch' federal approach; insisted 'Montana's senior water rights must be protected'

name: Brian Miller
what: Served as legal counsel for citizens challenging Quantica data center development in Yellowstone County; stated 'We need to have maximum local control and respect state sovereignty on data centers'; criticized NDAs hiding operational details

name: Michael Eisenhauer
what: Stated 'I think local control is the way it needs to be. I am not in favor of a mandate either for or against'; has 5-Pillar policy including closed-loop cooling, worker/ratepayer protections, and community final approval

name: Patrick McCracken
what: Stated 'most people would not want to live next door to a data center'; highlighted unaddressed electrical and water resource impacts; referenced Montana's constitutional guarantee of healthful environment

name: Adam B. Schiff
what: Introduced the Energy Cost Fairness and Reliability Act: large loads such as data centers pay 100% of the grid upgrades needed to serve them and bring their own generation before connecting.
source_name: Sen. Schiff unveils Energy Cost Fairness and Reliability Act (2026)

name: Peggy Flanagan
what: Forum News Service reported that she opposes major tax breaks for Big Tech, thinks NDA use for data centers should be banned, and says they should be built with union labor and meet Minnesota's environmental standards (all reporter's paraphrase), and quoted a statement from her: "Communities get to call the shots." The report said none of the four candidates it covered said they would support a statewide or federal moratorium.

name: Lauren Reinhold
what: Statement supporting community-approved projects with transparency and opposing tax breaks for data centers; 'there is no one-size-fits-all approach for this district'

name: Sharice Davids
what: Statement: 'no data center should move forward if it raises electricity costs for families, wastes our limited water resources, or shifts the burden onto Kansas communities'

name: Steve Scalise
what: Article says he highlights a Richland Parish, LA data center that paid every schoolteacher in the parish a $50,000 bonus. Quoted: 'They're good customers, they're good neighbors, and studies prove that they don't add to the cost of the grid. They're paying their own way.'

name: Brian Fitzpatrick
what: Per the Inquirer, his campaign spokesperson said he supports 'uniform federal regulations' and '100% control by local residents who could be impacted' and pointed to his cosponsorship of the Ratepayer Protection Act and the Data Center Transparency Act. The article notes his initial House vote for OBBBA (with a provision banning state/local AI regulation) and that he voted against the final version, which lacked the provision.

name: Chris Pappas
what: Told Spectrum News that New Hampshire is not the right place for AI data centers and that Granite Staters should not be asked to foot the bill for out-of-state corporations that might develop them.

name: Greg Stanton
what: Named as a cosponsor of the Responsible Data Center Siting Act, which would direct the Secretary of Energy to establish best practices for siting data centers considering energy availability, utility bills, water and electricity use, the environment, and community impacts such as noise.

name: Mike Levin
what: Listed as a cosponsor of H.R. 10321, the Responsible Data Center Siting Act of 2026 (sponsor Rep. Suhas Subramanyam), 'to direct the Secretary of Energy to establish best practices for the siting of data centers'.

name: Mary Peltola
what: Asked about data centers in Alaska after the Fairbanks Labor Day parade, Peltola said she takes her cue from the people of the region where a development is proposed and that if the region supports it, "who am I to stop it?" She added that broad concern about having enough electricity for ratepayers already on the grid, and about a huge new project making energy more challenging for households, "is a concern."

name: Stefany Shaheen
what: Stated 'I feel very strongly we need a moratorium. Our municipalities are not yet prepared to handle the complexity of what these kinds of projects could mean for their communities'

name: Mark Kelly
what: Co-signed a letter asking FERC to convene a technical conference on data-center load and affordable rates; previewed legislation to bring communities into siting with enforceable commitments.
source_name: Sen. Van Hollen & colleagues call on FERC to ensure affordable service amid data-center demand (2025)

name: Richard Blumenthal
what: Co-introduced the GRID Act to stop data centers from raising Americans' electricity costs.
source_name: Sens. Hawley & Blumenthal — GRID Act to stop data centers raising electric bills (2026)

name: Rick Scott
what: Introduced, with Marshall, a resolution endorsing the Ratepayer Protection Pledge: tech companies pay their own electricity and grid-infrastructure costs.
source_name: Sens. Rick Scott & Marshall introduce resolution supporting the Ratepayer Protection Pledge (2026)

name: Raphael G. Warnock
what: Led a letter to FERC to shield households from data-center costs, secured $50M for communities facing data-center energy and water demands, and called for a Georgia data-center pause.
source_name: Sens. Warnock & Markey push FERC to shield Americans from data-center energy costs (2026)

name: Richard J. Durbin
what: Cosponsored the Power for the People Act and introduced the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act (S. 4213).
source_name: Sen. Durbin introduces the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act (2026)

name: Roger Marshall
what: Introduced a resolution backing the Ratepayer Protection Pledge — tech companies pay their own grid costs — and opposes tax incentives for data centers.
source_name: Sen. Marshall applauds expansion of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge (2026)

name: Elizabeth Warren
what: Opened an investigation into whether Big Tech data centers raise families' utility bills and, with Hawley, secured mandatory EIA energy-use reporting for data centers.
source_name: Sen. Warren — investigation into Big Tech data centers' role in utility costs (2025)

name: Chris Van Hollen
what: Co-led the Power for the People Act with Welch: data-center operators pay the infrastructure and energy costs they create instead of ratepayers.
source_name: Sen. Welch joins bill so Americans aren't footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Angela D. Alsobrooks
what: Cosponsored the Power for the People Act, making data-center operators pay the grid costs they create.
source_name: Sen. Welch joins bill so Americans aren't footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Tina Smith
what: Cosponsored the Power for the People Act, making data-center operators pay the grid costs they create.
source_name: Sen. Welch joins bill so Americans aren't footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Josh Hawley
what: Co-introduced the GRID Act to stop data centers from raising Americans' electricity costs.
source_name: Sens. Hawley & Blumenthal — GRID Act to stop data centers raising electric bills (2026)

name: Cindy Hyde-Smith
what: Pressed FERC commissioners at oversight to make large loads such as data centers pay upfront so residential rates do not rise.
source_name: Sen. Hyde-Smith — FERC commissioners examine affordability as data centers proliferate (2026)

name: Jeanne Shaheen
what: Signed the New England senators' letter asking ISO New England how it will protect residential ratepayers from data-center-driven price increases.
source_name: Sen. Shaheen joins letter to ISO New England on data-center energy costs (2026)

name: Andy Kim
what: Co-led the NJ delegation's letter pressing PJM on the data-center-driven capacity price increase behind a ~17% rate rise.
source_name: Sens. Kim & Booker lead NJ delegation letter to PJM on rate increase (2025)

name: Martin Heinrich
what: Introduced the GRID Savings Act (2026) — large electricity users pay for grid infrastructure; opposes moratoriums as a race to the bottom.
source_name: Sen. Heinrich (ENR Ranking Member) — GRID Savings Act, large users pay for the grid (2026)

name: Jon Husted
what: Leads a Senate bill to protect Americans from footing the bill for new data centers.
source_name: Sen. Husted leads bill to protect Americans from new data-center costs (2026)

name: Ron Wyden
what: Demanded answers from Google, Apple, Meta and Amazon on data-center water use in Oregon, and proposed stripping data centers of federal investment incentives plus a new excise tax.
source_name: Sen. Wyden demands Big Tech execs answer on data-center water impact (2026)

name: John Fetterman
what: Blasted a proposed data-center moratorium as 'China First,' opposing the pause approach.
source_name: Sen. Fetterman calls a data-center moratorium 'China First' (2026)

name: Sheldon Whitehouse
what: Co-led the New England senators' letter to ISO New England on data-center-driven rate increases; earlier urged the White House not to fast-track data centers past clean-air, water and cost protections.
source_name: Sens. Reed & Whitehouse seek answers on how regional data centers could drive up costs (2026)

name: Mike Rounds
what: KOTA reported (paraphrase) that Rounds says data centers should be built only where local communities welcome them and, near term, through extensive dialogue with residents. His direct quotes on the page are about space: he said he believes the vast majority of new data centers will probably be based in space long-term.

name: Marsha Blackburn
what: Released the TRUMP AMERICA AI Act discussion draft, which would make data-center operators responsible for the full cost of energy and water infrastructure with no impact on ratepayers.
source_name: Sen. Blackburn unveils TRUMP AMERICA AI Act national policy framework (2025)

name: Mike Lee
what: As Energy Committee chair, backed FERC's Large Load Order at oversight and agreed existing ratepayers should not subsidize data centers; says data-center legislation is not currently a priority.
source_name: APPA — Senate ENR Committee holds FERC oversight hearing (2026)

name: Bernard Sanders
what: Introduced the AI Data Center Moratorium Act (S. 4214) with Rep. Ocasio-Cortez: no new or expanded AI data centers until federal safeguards, including against higher utility costs, are in place.
source_name: Sens. Sanders & Rep. Ocasio-Cortez announce AI Data Center Moratorium Act (2026)

name: Peter Welch
what: Joined a bill to ensure Americans aren't footing the bill for big data centers.
source_name: Sen. Welch joins bill so Americans aren't footing big data-center costs (2026)

name: Roy Cooper
what: Campaign issue page "Lowering Energy & Utility Costs" (last updated 2026-09-05) pledges to make data centers pay the full cost of the power they use, encourage large tech companies to build their own energy sources, involve local communities fully in any decision, and ban utility disconnections during dangerous heat and cold.

name: Katie Boyd Britt
what: Told Semafor she would "love to see" the Ratepayer Protection Pledge "turned into law," and that "we do not need a national moratorium, and we do not need a data center on every corner."

name: Bernie Moreno
what: At the Ohio Energy Affordability Summit announced he will introduce legislation imposing a federal tax equal to 100% of any state or local tax incentive given to a data center, saying "I don't want a single taxpayer dollar going to support these data centers."

name: James C. Justice
what: At the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce annual meeting, urged attendees not to fear data centers but said companies must be responsible neighbors: 'If you're going to come to West Virginia and you're going to do something in West Virginia, you need to be taking care of everybody. The environment, the water, the electricity bills, the noise. You've got to take care of everybody, and there's a way to do it.'

name: Brad Finstad
what: Said data centers "can play an important role in our economic future and national security, but the decision...should be made by the people and local leaders who know their communities best, not handed down by Washington"; emphasized need for corporate transparency.

name: Tom Emmer
what: MinnPost reported Emmer “immediately embraced” Trump’s message of support for data centers. In a post on X he said Trump was “absolutely spot on” and that “Communist China and our adversaries would love it if the United States was asleep at the wheel and stopped innovating and developing AI and emerging tech.”

name: Maggie Goodlander
what: Debate (WMUR, via InDepthNH): said some communities are seeing more than 200% increases in energy prices because of data centers; people and communities 'have got to have the ultimate say in whether a data center comes into their community'; reporter paraphrases her as calling for transparency and accountability and for the corporations to pay rather than taxpayers.

name: Paige Beauchemin
what: Debate (WMUR, via InDepthNH): reporter says she supports stopping the construction of any data centers until legislation can be introduced to regulate the issue; quoted: 'Those kinds of regulations need to ensure that environmental impact studies initially and ongoing, they need to ensure that utility costs are paid for by the companies and not from the other folks, and we also need to make sure that the local folks have their own local control.'

name: Tommy Tuberville
what: Op-ed "My game plan for data centers": "Local communities will decide whether a data center is right for them"; data centers go in "Alabama's highest property-tax bracket" with no abatements; companies must "pay the total cost of the transmission lines, substations and water systems" they need; pledges to freeze Alabama Power rates through 2029 and beyond.

name: Katie Boyd Britt
what: Defended the Trump administration's nonbinding Ratepayer Protection Pledge as "an outstanding first step to protecting Alabamians and ratepayers," and said communities should weigh "the amount of power that's taken" against tax revenue.

name: Pete Ricketts
what: At the Nebraska State Fair U.S. Senate debate, said local control governs data centers and that communities considering one should negotiate first, insisting on no impact on power rates and on water conservation through closed-loop systems, and can then ask for more in property taxes.

name: Bruce Westerman
what: Town hall: 'We are in a Cold War with China on developing AI technology'; 'we have to develop AI. To develop AI, you have to have data centers'; on water, 'I don't think is as big an issue as what some people make it out to be'; said data center companies 'are willing to pay for that new generating equipment' and transmission, and that communities should define water and electrical requirements and hold the companies accountable.

name: Lauren Boebert
what: Asked by a MeidasTouch reporter about Trump saying data center opponents are 'backwards and poor,' said 'The president says a lot of things. Sometimes, it's really funny... Anyway, I fought for data centers to have local control' and 'I want people to have local control. That's what I fought for.'

name: Steve Scalise
what: Told Fox Business: 'We are investigating whether China is behind a lot of this misinformation, false information against data centers,' and said Republicans are 'finding some things,' including Beijing-controlled social media bots.

name: Lily Tang Williams
what: GOP debate (WMUR, via InDepthNH): 'I would say no government perks, credits and taxpayer dollars should be involved. If a private company wants to come here, build data centers, then they need to respect our local control and address our concerns of environmental impact and electricity costs.'

name: Tim Burchett
what: Responded to Trump's warning that communities rejecting data centers risk becoming 'backwards and poor' by saying 'I guess I'm backwards and poor.' Called for more local control and suggested putting data centers in military installations.

name: John Fetterman
what: Posted on X, as quoted by the Philadelphia Inquirer, that he agreed with President Trump's defense of data centers: "There's nothing more damaging to a Democrat than agreeing with Trump AND data centers — but what's right is right," and "We must win the war for AI supremacy over China."

name: John Thune
what: Told KELOLAND that data centers 'need to be self-sufficient. They ought to be able to take care of their own utilities, their own power, and that ought to be a given any place they go in the country. But they shouldn't be going places where there isn't support for them at the local level.'

name: Kurt Alme
what: Responding to a Truth Social post in which President Trump said communities opposing data centers would end up "backwards and poor", told MTN he understood Trump's interest in economic development but that communities should make their own decisions. He called transparency, local hiring and protecting the community important guardrails, said companies will need to be open about electricity and water impacts (paraphrase), and said the Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed by Gov. Gianforte had positive steps but more could be done (paraphrase). He also cited tax-base opportunities and the benefits of innovation.

name: Stephanie Bice
what: Statement responding to President's comments on data centers: 'it is vital that local communities have a voice in the decisions on proposed data centers'; applauded Oklahoma legislature for passing ratepayer protection and groundwater laws

name: Roy Cooper
what: Fox News quoted him from an unnamed local interview saying data centers must pay for their own power and should build their own energy sources, and reported his campaign says local communities should have the final say on new projects, including local moratoriums. Fox described this as a shift from his time as governor and noted he has not called for an outright ban.

name: Raphael G. Warnock
what: Speaking in Guyton near OpenAI's proposed Effingham County site, called for a data center pause in Georgia — "In the absence of Congress not getting its act together and putting some common-sense guardrails in place, local communities and states find themselves in a race to the bottom" — with conditions: no increase in residents' water or electric bills, no water/air/noise/light pollution, no NDAs, no "sweetheart tax giveaways"; "This is not OpenAI County — this is Effingham County."

name: Michael Rulli
what: On Fox Business's Mornings with Maria, said 'Most of my constituents do not like data centers. They don't want them.' Told constituents to learn 'in front of the meter' (you pay) vs 'behind the meter' (the company pays) and whether the water system is self-contained, said data centers 'shouldn't put them on waste lands, brown fields' and 'Keep them out of the corn fields. Keep them out of the neighborhoods. We need to do better.' Also said 'The CCP has infiltrated Ohio with propaganda against this.' Did not state a position on the OpenAI/Nvidia project by name.

name: Roy Cooper
what: Campaign position via a spokesperson to Spectrum News: data centers must pay for all the energy they use without passing costs to consumers. Spectrum reported both he and his opponent support letting local communities block data centers and neither has voiced support for a federal moratorium; that numerous data centers were built while he was governor; and that his campaign says the tax breaks were signed in 2006 and expanded in 2015, before his term.

name: Kweisi Mfume
what: Added as a cosponsor of H.R. 9442, the AI Data Center Moratorium Act (sponsor Rep. Ocasio-Cortez), on 08/27/2026.

name: Josh Brecheen
what: Town hall, McAlester: said operators 'have to make sure that they are not driving up people's electricity costs'; 'Congress is not gonna create the regulatory environment. What we can do is make sure people have information about the data centers.' Co-sponsors HR9019 requiring the Energy Secretary to report to Congress on data center electricity and water use.

name: Ted Cruz
what: On NewsNation's 'Katie Pavlich Tonight', Cruz said 'the concerns being raised about data centers are real and reasonable' and suggested developers offer residents direct payments or tell them 'your electricity bill is zero for the rest of your life. We will pay your electric bill—forever.'

name: Gabe Vasquez
what: Per his Aug 25 release, was 'the only statewide or federal official' to publicly call for an end to the Socorro County data center proposal; the developer pulled out and commissioners unanimously approved a one-year moratorium.

name: Gabe Vasquez
what: Announced support for the FAIR Data Act (H.R. 9655), which would force large corporate electricity users to pay their own way so residential customers and small businesses do not cover data center costs.

name: John Fetterman
what: Posted on X, as quoted by TribLive: "AI supremacy and energy dominance underpins our national security" and "I reject the political pandering and hyperbole over data centers," adding "America must lead in the development of AI, otherwise we live under China's rules."

name: John Barrasso
what: On a proposal to site data centers on public lands, told Cowboy State Daily: 'Development of federal land, including the construction of new data centers, deserves meaningful input from state and local governments and the public. The people of Wyoming expect to have their voices heard.'

name: James Talarico
what: Responding to Ken Paxton's data-center platform, said Paxton had taken data-center industry money, voted for the tax break, and 'refused to use his power as attorney general to respond to Texans' requests to block data center development in their communities' (a reference, per the Tribune, to Hood County's pending request for an opinion on a county moratorium). The Tribune describes Talarico's plan as going further than Paxton's by giving local officials approval power, and also reports that Reid Hoffman gave $10 million to a super PAC supporting Talarico.

name: Paul LePage
what: Said 'I'm a big, big fan of data centers... I think they're going to create jobs. I think we can solve our energy problems' at a former mill site in Lincoln; downplayed water and power concerns. His campaign said Friday he supports 'sensible regulation,' including guarantees of adequate water supply, local community buy-in and no rate hikes for consumers.

name: Matthew Dunlap
what: Campaign warned 'if we don't approach these projects deliberately they will jack up energy prices'; favors developing benchmarks and standards for worker benefits, ratepayer impact, and community benefits

name: Melanie Stansbury
what: Formal letter to five NM state officials demanding written answers on Project Jupiter's water use, water rights, permits, and Rio Grande Compact compliance; called it 'an important test case for how New Mexico evaluates major industrial water users'

name: Bill Cassidy
what: Quoted praising Meta's Richland Parish data center: 'Economic growth increases the tax base and sales tax revenue' and 'Teacher bonuses there are up to $50,000 this year.'

name: Sherrod Brown
what: In an interview reported by Ohio Capital Journal, said Husted had “been the front guy on all these data centers, 200 in Ohio, getting huge over-the-top tax breaks, and raising utility rates,” and that no one should pay higher electric rates because out-of-state corporations put data centers in Ohio.

name: Katie Boyd Britt
what: Said data center decisions "need to be made on a local level," that communities that reject a proposal "shouldn't be forced" to proceed, and that neither "a data center on every corner" nor "a full moratorium" is the right avenue; backs the White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

name: John Thune
what: In an August 2026 South Dakota appearance, Thune called energy permitting reform a rare bipartisan opportunity, citing utilities' rapidly growing demand 'including that associated with data centers'; he framed faster permitting as the way to add generation and transmission.
source_name: KOTA Territory TV / South Dakota Searchlight

name: Tom Barrett
what: Introduced H.R. 10119, the Protecting Local Control of Data Centers Act (prohibits federal agencies from overriding local land-use, zoning, siting or permitting authority related to data centers and from leveraging federal funds to force local governments to give up that authority) and H.R. 10118, the No Data Center NDAs Act (prohibits members of Congress from signing NDAs about data centers, including locations or expected water and energy use). "They deserve to know all the facts and have the final say over any proposed project." His release says that in the Michigan House he voted against legislation giving data center construction and equipment tax breaks.

name: Susan M. Collins
what: Told the Bangor Daily News data-center projects should be handled case by case, favoring former mill sites because "there is usually hydropower right there," while saying "I do share the concern of data centers gobbling up too much energy and putting stress on the cost of energy."

name: Steven Horsford
what: At a town hall on AI and automation with Khanna, advocated advance notice and training for workers and collective bargaining as accountability tools (about worker automation, not data centers).

name: Darline Graham
what: In the South Carolina GOP Senate debate said: "Obviously, I just said I'm for data centers, but I also said that there needs to be community involvement, community guidelines, community guardrails."

name: Mike Lawler
what: On Fox Business's Mornings with Maria, said of Hochul's data center pause: 'What she is saying is, don't come here. Go do your business elsewhere, which is why New York State leads the nation in out-migration.' Also said New York has 'the highest tax burden and the worst business climate'.

name: Jen Kiggans
what: Told The Daily Signal: “They have data centers under the ocean floor. We can’t ban all data centers,” adding there is a “commonsense conversation to be had” on their use of energy, water and other local resources, that the debate has so far been left to Virginia’s Legislature, and that she has “enjoyed watching the Democrats fight with each other about the issue.”

name: Dina Titus
what: Asked Gov. Lombardo to refrain from approving data center tax abatements for projects on BLM land until the Legislature reconvenes to reconsider; the governor's reply did not commit to halting abatements.

name: Pat Fallon
what: Told CBS News Texas: 'I think it was a thoughtful, good step that the governor put in place. He was listening to his constituents... They share those concerns, as I do.' Referring to Abbott's data center directives, which CBS describes as including a pause.

name: JoAnna Mendoza
what: Said: 'No data centers in the desert... Not right now, not in our district, not in our state.' Also said 'We can't have data centers near residential areas,' citing ASU research that air-cooled data centers emit heat 'anywhere between two to four degrees more,' and warned energy bills would go up.

name: Andrea Salinas
what: Introduced Data Center Community Reinvestment Act establishing 1-cent-per-kWh excise tax on data center electricity consumption (>1 MW capacity), directing $1.76B/year to Land and Water Conservation Fund, Housing Trust Fund, Superfund, Highway Trust Fund, and Energy Technology Trust Fund

name: Gabe Vasquez
what: Cosponsor of H.R. 9825, the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act of 2026 (sponsor Rep. Underwood), whose official title is to require data center operators to submit reports on data center energy and water use; added as a cosponsor 08/13/2026.

name: Dan Sullivan
what: Asked in Kodiak about a rumored Navy data center at the Naval Special Warfare detachment on Spruce Cape, said "I had never heard of that issue until last week," "I think it's a rumor," and "if it's true, I think it's a bad idea and I will work to stop it."

name: Amy Klobuchar
what: In a KFGO interview during her run for governor said data centers "cause people's rates to go up, they have hurt the environment, and that just can't keep happening," criticized non-disclosure agreements keeping projects "in the dark," and called for local control over siting decisions.

name: Shelley Moore Capito
what: In a Roll Call story on the Tucker County data-center fight, a Capito spokesperson said in a statement that she has emphasized local involvement, responsible stewardship and protection of utility payers alongside job creation and community development, and that she remains in touch with local leaders. Spokesperson's statement, not Capito's own words. The same story says the group Tucker United reached out to members of Congress who represent the area and had not received a response.

name: Adrian Smith
what: At Nebraska energy summit: 'The efficiencies that can be achieved already with AI, it's amazing... We should not stand in the way. We should celebrate how much better lives can be with more economic efficiency out there that can be a result of AI.' Article reports the delegation advocated for data centers while a dozen-plus counties weighed moratoriums, and that members said AI should have rules without specifics.

name: Rand Paul
what: During a visit to Fort Knox, on data center siting: 'I don't think the federal government should regulate where data centers are placed or built, nor do I think the governor should. Each county should make this decision at the most local level.' He added that counties with a large tax base might not want one while poorer counties might.

name: Bill Hagerty
what: Asked by WBIR in Knoxville about AI data centers (which the station notes several East Tennessee governments have placed 12-month moratoriums on), said 'we made it very clear to the data centers that they're going to have to make the investment, not only in our capacity but in our grid and support all of that.'

name: Luke Bronin
what: Victory speech called for 'sensible artificial intelligence regulation'; published platform says 'We need guardrails' against algorithmic addiction of kids and 'machines that act without human input or oversight'. The article records no data-center position.

name: Paul Tonko
what: Said at an Albany roundtable that data centers like the one proposed for the Kenwood site in South Albany "should be built in communities that want them", and that "we have to provide for those safety nets and the guardrails for both AI and data centers."

name: Sherrod Brown
what: Ohio Capital Journal reports that Brown attacked Husted's support for data-center tax breaks in two July ads and, in a third, promised to make data centers pay the full cost of their electricity use; that he has called to end the data center tax breaks and says local communities should have a say on construction; and that he has not embraced a halt in construction.

name: Sherrod Brown
what: In a statement to Ohio Capital Journal, said Ohioans should not be forced to subsidize data-center costs and that Ohioans should get to decide whether data centers are built in their community.

name: Sherrod Brown
what: Ohio Capital Journal reports that Brown, in a June Spectrum News interview, said data center operators have to process water properly and recirculate it; and that as a first-term senator in 2010 he secured $2.8 million for a Dayton-area research center developing water cooling technology for large data centers.

name: Ron Wyden
what: As Finance Committee ranking member released a white paper proposing to remove existing tax investment incentives as applied to data centers and create a Data Center Public Investment excise tax, with revenue for workers displaced by AI; said communities "are rightfully questioning whether the rapid buildout of data centers across the nation will benefit them, as local disruptions rise."

name: Ro Khanna
what: Introduced the Data Center Bill of Rights resolution: communities may ban data centers in residential areas and within 2,500 feet of homes, schools, childcare, hospitals or nursing homes; may reject a project through a transparent community process; county and municipal authority to prohibit or regulate is preserved against state preemption; and every data center must use clean, reliable energy under strict noise and air limits. It is a resolution, so it does not itself change law.

name: Ace Parsi
what: Said at a virtual 'Candidates Against Transmission Lines' news conference: 'People don't feel like they're listened to or represented, because if nobody wants these, how did this go through such an overwhelming majority in the House and Senate.' Said the architects behind the data-center build-out have been withholding information. (HB 2014 repeal was called for by another candidate, Vince George.)

name: Chuck Gray
what: At a Sheridan forum said: 'I'm the only candidate on stage that has been talking about these data AI data centers and expressed my opposition to these AI data centers.' Reporter: only Gray has indicated a desire to ban them at the federal level.

name: Chuck Gray
what: Same article: Rasner said Gray voted in 2021 for data-center tax breaks; the article confirms Gray voted to keep the tax exemption, and that his signature is on the business registration approval for Terra Crypto, tied by a 2024 order to MineOne, which Gray denied wrongdoing over.

name: Eugene Vindman
what: Introduced the Smart Data Center Policy Act, directing the Department of Commerce to study the costs, benefits and possible federal incentives for siting data centers in industrial zones, rail and airport hubs and military installations rather than near homes and green space, with findings due to Congress in 180 days. Vindman: “We need to ensure data centers pay their fair share and are built in places that make sense — not next to neighborhoods, schools, or our public lands.”

name: Amy Klobuchar
what: Through spokesman Darwin Forsyth, said she "supports robust environmental standards for any proposed data centers as well as greater transparency and local control over decisions to build," called Minnesota's 2025 law requiring data centers to pay the full cost of their energy use "a good start," and said her focus would be protecting Minnesotans' energy bills and water; she did not answer questions on local moratoriums or NDAs.

name: Shomari Figures
what: At a Lowndes County event asked residents if they wanted the proposed 1,050-acre, $1.5B AI data center in Hayneville; when they said no, said 'Well, I'm with the people of Lowndes County.' Columnist reports he is not entirely opposed to hyperscale data centers but says companies need to pick sites where communities actually want them.

name: Dina Titus
what: Nevada Independent: described the permitting process she wants for data centers on federal land as 'Full environmental permitting process with consideration for water and also public consultation and hearings'.

name: Carrie Buck
what: NV Independent survey: federal government should 'make it easier to build the energy and infrastructure America needs to lead in AI'

name: Teresa Benitez-Thompson
what: NV Independent survey: does not want federal actions to prevent state or local governments from taking their own regulatory action on data centers

name: David Flippo
what: NV Independent survey: 'The best decisions are made at the most local level possible.' Opposes tax abatements; would support federal involvement only for national security protection

name: Susie Lee
what: Nevada Independent: said there should be disclosure requirements on water consumption and potentially energy efficiency standards. The article reports almost all candidates opposed a blanket federal pause on data centers.

name: Martin O'Donnell
what: NV Independent survey: supports legislation ensuring local communities are not negatively affected by data centers; backs water usage disclosure requirements

name: Steven Horsford
what: Nevada Independent: said the federal government should set standards requiring disclosure of energy and water use; states should be allowed to 'go further' ('a national standard should act as a floor we can build on, never a ceiling'). The only candidate who kept the door open to a federal moratorium in future.

name: Cody Whipple
what: Nevada Independent: written response supports 'common-sense frameworks that safeguard Nevada's natural resources while fostering technological innovation'; campaign later said he wants local water, agricultural and technology officials to inform federal standards. At a closed-door event recording he called data centers a 'national security issue for us'.

name: Abdul El-Sayed
what: E&E News reported that in a televised WOOD-TV primary debate in July he said he would make his terms of engagement law, called for a community benefits agreement with the money put in escrow, and said officials should be able to shut down non-compliant data centers. The article said he had not endorsed a nationwide data-center moratorium.

name: James Talarico
what: At a San Antonio stop, said data centers that will not create good union jobs 'shouldn't be in our communities'; the paper reports (paraphrase) that he told reporters he does not support a total moratorium on new data-center construction and prefers regulation.

name: Hillary Scholten
what: Announced introduction of two bills, the Data Center Resource Disclosure Act (NTIA annual survey of operators' energy and water consumption, public comment, public dashboard, list of non-responders) and the Defending Our Energy and Water Act (DoD to update data center efficiency requirements and ensure new facilities adopt cooling technologies that reduce water impact). "Accountability starts with transparency."

name: Don Beyer
what: Letter urging the Fairfax County Planning Commission to deny the Edsall Data Center Substation 2232 application, citing land use, flooding mitigation, light and noise pollution and Lincolnia's growth goals: "Data center infrastructure should not be built in residential areas where its scale and likely impacts are fundamentally incompatible with the character and quality of life of adjacent neighborhoods."

name: Andy Barr
what: Quoted in the Department of Energy's announcement of the Paducah Site data center campus (a more than $100 billion private investment), calling it historic and saying he personally advocated with the Energy Secretary to make the project happen.
source_name: U.S. Department of Energy press release

name: Chris Van Hollen
what: Signed, with Sen. Alsobrooks and seven Maryland House members, a letter urging FERC to relieve Maryland ratepayers of transmission costs assigned for out-of-state data center demand and to require PJM to adopt stronger protections.
source_name: Rep. April McClain Delaney press release (joint delegation letter)

name: Angela D. Alsobrooks
what: Signed, with Sen. Van Hollen and seven Maryland House members, a letter urging FERC to act quickly on the Maryland Office of People's Counsel complaint and to require PJM to protect Maryland ratepayers from transmission costs assigned to them for out-of-state data center demand.
source_name: Rep. April McClain Delaney press release (joint delegation letter)

name: Jon Husted
what: Told Spectrum News "What we're requiring the data centers to do is to produce their own power so that the local ratepayers don't have to foot the bill," and that data-center siting decisions "should be made by local residents and local communities, not the federal government."

name: David McCormick
what: In a City & State Q&A reposted by his office, described an "AI covenant" for data centers: "You need to protect rates for the people in the community... give them rate protection or bring more energy than you use," "You need to protect the water... via a closed loop," and "The ultimate decision-making power is going to reside with the communities – township supervisors, county commissioners and the people."
source_name: City & State PA (via Sen. McCormick site)

name: Johnny Olszewski
what: Co-signed Maryland Congressional delegation letter to FERC urging revision of PJM cost-allocation rules so Maryland consumers do not finance $2B in infrastructure built primarily for out-of-state data centers.

name: Sarah Elfreth
what: Co-signed Maryland Congressional delegation letter to FERC urging revision of PJM cost-allocation rules so Maryland consumers do not finance $2B in infrastructure built primarily for out-of-state data centers.

name: Glenn Ivey
what: Co-signed Maryland Congressional delegation letter to FERC urging revision of PJM cost-allocation rules so Maryland consumers do not finance $2B in infrastructure built primarily for out-of-state data centers.

name: April McClain Delaney
what: Joined, and issued the press release for, the Maryland Congressional delegation letter to FERC urging revision of PJM transmission cost-allocation rules so Maryland ratepayers do not pay roughly $2 billion for infrastructure needed primarily for out-of-state data centers; letter supports the Maryland Office of People's Counsel's FERC complaint.

name: Kweisi Mfume
what: Named among the Maryland congressional delegation members calling on FERC to require PJM to protect Marylanders after PJM assigned roughly $2 billion in costs to Maryland ratepayers for infrastructure needed primarily to serve out-of-state data centers; the letter supports a complaint filed by the Maryland Office of People's Counsel.

name: Jamie Raskin
what: Co-signed Maryland Congressional delegation letter to FERC urging revision of PJM cost-allocation rules so Maryland consumers do not finance $2B in infrastructure built primarily for out-of-state data centers.

name: Peggy Flanagan
what: In the MPR News DFL primary debate with Rep. Angie Craig, said of data centers that it is troubling to be moving at the speed of corporate interests rather than community. MPR reported she said residents across Minnesota and the country have big concerns about data centers. Her "existential threat" remark in the same debate was, per MPR, about AI getting out of control.

name: Roger Marshall
what: Press release applauding the expansion of the Ratepayer Protection Pledge: 'I've heard from Kansans who are concerned that infrastructure costs for data centers could be pushed onto households, small businesses, schools, hospitals, and farms.'

name: Raphael G. Warnock
what: Wrote EPA Administrator Zeldin requesting best-practice guidance for communities protecting water supplies from data center expansion, with a written response and briefing within four weeks: "Small, rural communities have been left to negotiate on their own with multi-million-dollar corporations whose well-staffed legal teams may negotiate dozens of deals at a time." Cited OpenAI's Effingham County project and 24 Georgia local moratoria.

name: Cindy Hyde-Smith
what: At the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee's FERC oversight hearing, said Mississippi "continues to be at the forefront of safeguarding ratepayers by ensuring companies, like data centers, pay their fair share for large loads," and asked commissioners what mechanisms FERC is implementing for large-load customers to make upfront payments and minimum financial commitments to keep rates from rising.

name: Tim Scott
what: Authored a Post and Courier commentary saying data centers are vital to competitiveness and national security, that "Hardworking families and small businesses should not have higher electric bills because of the energy demands of massive global corporations," and praising Google's commitment to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge to secure 100% of its added energy needs without passing costs to ratepayers.
source_name: The Post and Courier (op-ed by Sen. Scott)

name: Mark R. Warner
what: Said local governments' deals with data centers should be public before any benefits are granted: 'all the non-disclosure agreements need to be disclosed so the community can make the judgment.' The article also reports his proposal would require data centers not to add to consumers' electric bills, use clean power including clean backup, meet water-use standards and keep setbacks from residential neighborhoods (reporter's description).

name: Rashida Tlaib
